Both figures only include the expected 23 detections, while negative samples were excluded from these analyses.

Thus, although hybrid-capture sequencing recovered reads from all expected targets, read presence was not sufficient to define a positive result or exclude false-positive detections, and genome coverage was a better correlating metric with viral load. We therefore aimed to develop platform-specific cut-offs incorporating abundance, genome coverage and the relative signal of each virus across samples to control for high viral load sample bleeding and/or cross-contamination.

2. Platform-specific cut-offs removed most non-expected signals in EQA dataset

As we show in the previous section, probe-based viral metagenomic sequencing can detect very low-level signals, but not every signal should be interpreted as "presence" of a virus. Low read counts may arise from wet-lab contamination, index hopping, cross-sample contamination, or non-specific mapping. Therefore, we aimed to select stringent, data-driven cut-offs to distinguish reproducible viral detections from other false signals based on results of the routine diagnostics as reference, while preserving sensitivity for true positives. To define these cut-offs, we sampled 100,000 possible quasi-random parameter combinations separately for AVITI and ONT. Each combination sampled three cut-off values: I) how much of the viral genome was covered, II) how abundant the viral reads were (as read count or RPM), and III) whether the signal was strong enough relative to the highest signal for the same virus within the sample type, referred to as the bleed ratio. These candidate cut-off sets were evaluated on the clinical CSF and BAL datasets, and the best-performing parameter sets of 100 combinations were selected (see methods). These 100 best-performing parameters sets were then applied to the EQA datasets for external validation (Figure 3a). The selected optimal cutoffs were intentionally stringent (see methods and Supplementary methods) but remained permissive enough to retain high analytical sensitivity. The top 100 ranked parameter sets for each platform fell in a relatively narrow range for each parameter compared to the sampling range, which may indicate that the ranges are potentially a high-performing solution ranges rather than random combinations performing well as outliers (Figure 3b-c).

After application of the selected operational cut-offs on the EQA dataset, 22 of the 23 expected viral targets remained positive on each platform. AVITI did not retain human adenovirus 4 (HadV-4) in 2025 Sample 6, whereas ONT did not retain HSV-2 in 2024 Sample 6. The AVITI HadV-4 detection comprised 2,679 reads and 48.0% genome coverage but failed the bleed-ratio criterion because a high-abundance adenovirus-positive clinical sample was cosequenced in the same run and therefore provided the denominator for this calculation. Posthoc sequence-level comparison supported the HadV-4 signal as a genuine detection distinct from the potential donor sample, indicating that it was removed by a conservative bleed-ratio filter. Among non-expected sample-virus combinations with an observed raw sequencing signal, the selected cut-offs removed 53 of 56 AVITI signals (94.6%) and 29 of 30 ONT signals White circles show performance of the median cut-off set; red circles show performance of the selected operational cut-off set. "Detection sensitivity": detection capability of metagenomics when all virus detections are pooled regardless of the samples that they were identified from. "Sample sensitivity": Detection is deemed successful when every virus in one sample is detected. "Off-target removal" was defined as the proportion of observed raw non-expected sample-virus signals removed after cut-off application. "Diagnostic specificity": Metagenomics identifying negative samples as negative.

3. Sensitivity is sample type and viral load dependent

Because operational pathogen-calling cut-offs should reflect clinical sample matrices rather than artificial control material alone, the cut-offs were derived from the clinical CSF and BAL dataset. Using these cut-off values, we assessed routine-target performance in the same cohort of 14 CSF and 21 BAL specimens, using routine molecular diagnostic results as the reference standard. Detection-level sensitivity was defined per individual pathogen detection, whereas sample-level sensitivity required recovery of all expected viruses within a given sample.

Overall, AVITI corroborated 26 of 30 routine pathogen detections (86.7%), while ONT corroborated 25 of 30 (83.3%) (Figure 4a). Both platforms detected all routinely targeted pathogens in CSF samples (7/7). In BAL, detection-level sensitivity was 82.6% for AVITI (19/23) and 78.3% for ONT (18/23), while sample-level sensitivity was 71.4% for AVITI (10/14) and 64.3% for ONT (9/14). No routine-negative clinical samples showed retained viral detections after cut-off application, corresponding to 100% diagnostic specificity.

Because sensitivity was lower in BAL samples, we further examined the missed routine detections. All missed detections had Cq values above 32, with 3 of 4 AVITI misses and 2 of 5 ONT misses occurring above Cq 36. Below a Cq threshold of 36, AVITI reached 90% detection sensitivity; below a Cq threshold of 34, both platforms reached more than 90% detection sensitivity (Figure 4b). These findings indicate that clinical sensitivity was influenced by both viral load and sample type.

4. Viral metagenomics can identify overlooked pathogens and remove the biases of stepwise testing

To further examine discordant and additional viral findings, we summarized all PCR-tested sample-detected virus pairs together with the corresponding cut-off-filtered AVITI and ONT metagenomic results (Figure 5a). Among routinely targeted viruses, most detections were recovered by both sequencing platforms: 24 of 30 routine PCR-positive sample-virus pairs were detected by both AVITI and ONT. AVITI detected 26 of 30 routine targets overall, whereas ONT detected 25 of 30. Four routine PCR-positive detections were negative on reflex testing and were therefore shown separately (dark red in Figure 5a); these discordant reflex-negative results may reflect loss of detectable signal after sample handling or freeze-thawing, rather than true failure of metagenomic detection.

Metagenomic findings also prompted additional reflex PCR testing (shown as non-routine or reflex in Figure 5), particularly for highly prevalent herpesviruses in BAL samples, including EBV, HHV-6 and HHV-7. Among 35 non-routine PCR-positive detections, 17 were recovered by both sequencing platforms, while an additional 17 were recovered by AVITI only; no nonroutine detection was recovered by ONT alone, and one was missed by both methods. Thus, AVITI showed slightly higher routine-target sensitivity and recovered substantially more additional low-abundance non-routine detections than ONT (Figure 5b). Genome recovery also differed between platforms. Across the dataset, AVITI recovered 18 near-complete genomes (>=90% genome completeness), compared with 7 by ONT (Figure 5c). Among routine PCR-positive detections, near-complete genomes were recovered for 13 AVITI detections and 7 ONT detections. Among non-routine PCR-positive detections, AVITI recovered 5 nearcomplete genomes, whereas ONT recovered none.

The clinical relevance of additional EBV, HHV-6 and HHV-7 detections in BAL samples remains uncertain. In contrast, two CSF samples illustrated the potential value of broader viral detection (C2 and C4). In sample C4, routine testing identified JC polyomavirus with 2.87 log10 copies/mL. Metagenomics recovered JC polyomavirus at low genome completeness (8.4%) and additionally detected HHV-6 with a near-complete genome, which was confirmed by reflex PCR (Figure 5a). These findings suggest that stepwise CSF diagnostic algorithms may miss CNS-relevant viral targets that are detectable by broad metagenomic testing.

Discussion

In this study, we benchmarked hybrid-capture viral metagenomics using both short-read (AVITI) and long-read (ONT) sequencing across mock EQA samples and clinical CSF and BAL specimens, and developed a data-driven approach to define cut-offs for both platforms. We achieved 95.7% (22/23) detection-level sensitivity on EQA samples, 100% (7/7) sensitivity on clinical CSF routine targets, and high overall clinical routine-target sensitivity, reaching 86.7% for AVITI and 83.3% for ONT. For CSF, the observed sensitivity was higher than the pooled sensitivity reported in a recent meta-analysis of mNGS for infectious meningoencephalitis, 20 suggesting hybrid-capture enrichment may improve sensitivity in CSF samples, supporting the literature work on mock samples. 21 Sensitivity in BAL samples was lower, reaching 82.6% for AVITI and 78.3% for ONT at individual virus detection level, which we speculate that higher host DNA background in this sample type may be reducing capture efficiency during hybridization. An additional reason may be potential viral signal loss from freeze-thaw cycles prior to processing, which we show that four lower viral load detections were not detected when reflex-testing was conducted.

Despite expanding clinical use of viral mNGS, pathogen calling still relies on ad-hoc thresholds such as minimum read counts (often 1-2 reads), 2-3 non-overlapping regions of coverage, fixed RPM or percentage of total reads cut-offs, or simple fold-change over negative controls, with little consensus or formal justification. 22, 23 These heterogeneous and permissive rules may contribute to high sensitivity but widely variable specificity, which can drop to about 26% in severe pneumonia cohorts and shows broad inter-study spread in diagnostic test accuracy meta-analyses. 24, 25 Contamination-focused work shows that cross-sample bleed, index hopping and reagent "kitome" DNA are pervasive in viral mNGS, yet most studies still address them qualitatively rather than embedding them into quantitative decision thresholds. In our study, we present a Latin hypercube sampling approach that jointly optimizes genome coverage, abundance and bleed-ratio parameters to select best-performing cut-off values and potentially a plausible operating range, enabling more balanced comparisons between sequencing platforms instead of ad-hoc cut-offs. These cut-offs are not intended to be universal but are laboratory-and workflow-specific; when wet-lab protocols or bioinformatic pipelines change, repeating the same optimization procedure can help redefine appropriate operational thresholds in a transparent, data-driven way. Multiple CSF mNGS studies have shown that unbiased sequencing can reveal unexpected viral etiologies missed by stepwise testing, including Parvovirus B19, enteroviruses, hepatitis E virus and even vesiviruses in patients initially labelled as having idiopathic or autoimmune CNS disease. 1, 26 In our cohort, one sample similarly illustrated this added value: metagenomics identified HHV-6 with higher genome completeness alongside JC polyomavirus with lower genome completeness (which is the only virus reported in the routine diagnostics results), with HHV-6 only confirmed by reflex PCR. In BAL, we frequently observed EBV, HHV-6 and HHV-7, echoing mNGS studies that detect lower-respiratory herpesviruses in roughly onethird of immunocompetent pneumonia patients and associate them with longer hospital stays and potentially with immune status of the patients. 27 To our knowledge, this is the first direct head-to-head comparison of short-read and long-read sequencing performed on the same hybrid-captured viral libraries across both mock EQA panels and clinical specimens. Prior studies comparing sequencing technologies have either combined hybrid capture exclusively with short-read platforms or applied ONT to untargeted workflows, where sensitivity at low viral loads consistently lags behind Illumina-based approaches. 21 In our study, the performance gap was narrower than the literature suggests; both platforms achieved similar routine-target sensitivity and 100% specificity, though AVITI showed an advantage in low-abundance non-routine detection and genome recovery. This is potentially due to extra steps involved before ONT sequencing as well as sequencing depth difference between technologies rather than the sequencing itself. On the other hand, ONT's commonly cited speed benefit is also substantially narrowed in hybrid-capture workflows, where the 16-hour hybridization step dominates turnaround regardless of sequencer choice. Intrinsic differences in sequencing depth between the short-read sequencing run (6.9M reads per sample in our study) and the long-read flow cell (20k reads per sample in our study) should nonetheless be kept in mind when comparing results.

With sensitivity and specificity now more systematically addressable, cost and turnaround time remain the practical challenges for routine clinical implementation of viral metagenomics. Newer short-read platforms with lower read output but shorter runtime, advances in hybridization chemistry and emerging PCR-free on-flow-cell hybrid-capture approaches are collectively pushing total workflow time below two days. 28, 29 On the other hand, long-read technologies can be analyzed in real time which can provide data access before completion of the sequencing run. Additionally, short-read technology used in this study requires batching of multiple samples, whereas long-read technologies may use less number of samples being pooled together. On the other hand, even if sequencing may be conducted on a low-throughput sequencing platform for a low number of samples, hybridization still requires batching of multiple samples. Overall, while both platforms show technical feasibility, the choice between them should be informed by the tradeoffs, costs, and batching needs when multiple samples have to be sequenced.

Our study has limitations that should be acknowledged. The clinical cohort is small, and samples were processed from frozen material, which may have contributed to nucleic acid degradation and reduced sensitivity for some targets which we show with reflex PCR testing. Additionally, sample selection was based on the availability of residual material, diagnostic testing on CSF samples was not standardized, as tests were performed according to the clinician's request as part of standard clinical care. Furthermore, cut-offs were derived and evaluated using the same clinical cohort, which may have produced optimistic performance estimates. However, their performance on independent EQA panels suggests that the cut-offs retained discriminatory ability beyond the derivation cohort. That said, missed detections occurring at Cq values above 32 and only in BAL samples suggest that our sensitivity estimates reflect genuinely difficult samples rather than workflow failure, making them conservative rather than optimistic benchmarks for prospective clinical use. Moreover, our study offers a reproducible cut-off selection approach usable to any laboratory running similar workflows. Additionally, to our knowledge, this is the first parallel short-read and long-read comparison on the same hybrid-captured libraries across both controlled EQA samples and real clinical CSF and BAL samples.

Grey points show individual parameter sets, white open circles show the top-100 median parameter values, and red circles show the selected operational cut-offs. d. Detection sensitivity, sample sensitivity, observed off-target removal, and negative-sample specificity in the 12 EQA samples across the top 100 cut-off sets.White circles show performance of the median cut-off set; red circles show performance of the selected operational cut-off set. "Detection sensitivity": detection capability of metagenomics when all virus detections are pooled regardless of the samples that they were identified from. "Sample sensitivity": Detection is deemed successful when every virus in one sample is detected. "Off-target removal" was defined as the proportion of observed raw non-expected sample-virus signals removed after cut-off application. "Diagnostic specificity": Metagenomics identifying negative samples as negative.

Detection sensitivity reflects individual sample-virus targets; sample sensitivity reflects the percentage of samples in which all expected targets were detected.
